title: Best Budget Home Theater Receiver (2026): 6 Cheap AVRs Ranked
metaDescription: The best budget home theater receiver picks for 5.1 and 5.1.2 Atmos, ranked by what each tier gets you: 4K/120 HDMI, room EQ and honest watts.
keywords: best budget receiver for home theater
best budget av receiver for home theater
intro:
The best budget home theater receiver for most people is the **[Denon AVR-S770H](/gear/denon-avr-s770h/)**: it is the least expensive receiver here that ticks all four boxes that matter in 2026, namely seven channels for 5.1.2 Dolby Atmos, 4K/120-capable HDMI, automatic room calibration and Wi-Fi streaming. This page is for buyers who want a real surround system without paying for features they won't use.

Cheap receivers cut corners in predictable places: fewer channels, simpler room EQ, older HDMI, inflated power ratings. We rank each pick by what you give up, not just what it costs. If you only need 5.1, the **[Yamaha RX-V4A](/gear/yamaha-rx-v4a/)** is the smarter buy, and the **[Sony STR-DH590](/gear/sony-str-dh590/)** is the cheapest sensible receiver for a basic setup.
quickAnswer: The Denon AVR-S770H is the best budget home theater receiver: 7.2 channels for 5.1.2 Atmos, HDMI 2.1 with 4K/120, Audyssey calibration and HEOS streaming. For a 5.1 system, the Yamaha RX-V4A adds 4K/120 gaming support for less. The Sony STR-DH590 is the cheapest worthwhile option, but it has no Atmos or Wi-Fi.

picks.body:
The AVR-S770H is Denon's entry-level 7.2 receiver, and it's the cheapest model here that doesn't force a hard compromise. Denon rates it at **75 W per channel (8 ohms, 20 Hz–20 kHz, two channels driven)**, it has **seven amplified channels** and **two subwoofer outputs**, and it decodes **Dolby Atmos and DTS:X** for a **5.1.2** layout.

You get **six HDMI inputs** with HDMI 2.1 support for 4K/120 gaming, plus **eARC** so your TV's streaming apps can send lossless Atmos to the receiver. Streaming is covered by HEOS, AirPlay 2 and Bluetooth, and calibration is **Audyssey MultEQ** with the included mic.

The trade-off: basic MultEQ uses lower-resolution filters than the MultEQ XT in the [Denon AVR-X1800H](/gear/denon-avr-x1800h/), so bass correction is less precise, and the X1800H's extra 5 W per channel is meaningless by comparison (0.3 dB). If you have a single subwoofer in an average living room, the S770H's correction is fine. If you have two subs or a boomy room, stretch to the X1800H.

Who it suits: anyone building a first Atmos system with bookshelf or tower speakers and two up-firing modules, such as the [Klipsch R-41SA](/gear/klipsch-r-41sa/). It's the best budget AV receiver for home theater because nothing cheaper gets you 5.1.2 and modern HDMI together.

If your room only has space for five speakers and a sub, the RX-V4A is the better value than any 7.2 model. It has **five amplified channels**, **two subwoofer outputs** and **four HDMI 2.1 inputs** that support **8K/60 and 4K/120**, which is unusual at this level and means your console can run 120 Hz through the receiver.

Yamaha rates it at **80 W per channel, measured into 6 ohms** (20 Hz–20 kHz, 0.06% THD, two channels driven). That 6-ohm test load is easy to miss; into 8-ohm speakers, output will be somewhat lower. Pair it with speakers of 87 dB sensitivity or better, such as the [Polk Monitor XT20](/gear/polk-monitor-xt20/), and you'll have plenty of level for a living room.

**YPAO** calibration, **MusicCast** multiroom, AirPlay 2 and Bluetooth make it a capable music receiver too. The trade-off is that five channels mean **no height speakers**: it decodes Atmos but plays it on ear-level speakers only. If overhead sound matters to you, the [Denon AVR-S770H](/gear/denon-avr-s770h/) is the minimum.

Compared with the [Sony STR-DH590](/gear/sony-str-dh590/) below it, the RX-V4A adds HDMI 2.1, eARC, Wi-Fi and better room EQ. It's the best budget 5.1 home theater receiver for gamers.

The STR-DH590 is a no-frills **5.2-channel** receiver for people who want to connect five speakers and a sub to a TV and be done. It has **four HDMI inputs** with **4K HDR passthrough**, Bluetooth for phone streaming, two subwoofer outputs and Sony's auto-calibration with the included mic.

It's also the best example on this page of why power ratings need reading carefully. Sony often quotes power for its budget receivers at **6 ohms and 1 kHz**, a less demanding test that produces a bigger number than the full-bandwidth, two-channel, 8-ohm ratings Denon and Yamaha publish. Treat it as a modest amplifier suited to a small or medium room with reasonably efficient speakers.

The trade-offs are significant: **no Dolby Atmos or DTS:X decoding**, **no Wi-Fi streaming**, **no 4K/120** passthrough and **ARC rather than eARC** on the HDMI output. Connect your console directly to the TV and send audio back to the receiver; you'll still get Dolby Digital and DTS 5.1, which is what most streaming and broadcast content uses anyway.

Who it suits: a bedroom or den system, a first surround setup on the tightest budget, or someone pairing it with a speaker package like the [Klipsch Reference Theater Pack](/gear/klipsch-reference-theater-pack/). If you can stretch, the [Yamaha RX-V4A](/gear/yamaha-rx-v4a/) is a far more future-proof cheap home theater receiver.

picks.award: Best Budget Receiver With Dirac Live
picks.body:
The TX-NR6100 brings **Dirac Live** room correction (added via firmware) and **THX Certified Select** status to a mid-priced 7.2 receiver. Onkyo rates it at **100 W per channel (8 ohms, 20 Hz–20 kHz, 0.08% THD, two channels driven)** and also quotes **210 W** at 6 ohms, 1 kHz, 10% THD with one channel driven, a perfect illustration of how the same amp can carry two very different numbers.

Seven channels give you **5.1.2 Atmos or 7.1**, with HDMI 2.1 inputs for 4K/120 gaming and eARC on the output. Out of the box it uses Onkyo's AccuEQ calibration; Dirac Live is the reason to choose it, because it lets you set your own target curve and corrects timing as well as frequency response. Check the current Dirac licence terms when you buy, as bandwidth options and pricing have changed over time.

The trade-off: the Onkyo app and menus are less polished than Denon's or Yamaha's, and the brand's ownership changes in recent years make some buyers wary about long-term firmware support. Against the [Denon AVR-X1800H](/gear/denon-avr-x1800h/), you get better potential room correction and 20 W more per channel (about 1 dB); the Denon wins on ease of use. For tinkerers with tricky rooms, this is the best affordable home theater receiver.

The AVR-X1800H is what the [Denon AVR-S770H](/gear/denon-avr-s770h/) becomes when you spend a bit more, and the upgrade is mostly about calibration. You get **Audyssey MultEQ XT** instead of basic MultEQ, which uses higher-resolution correction filters and up to eight mic positions, plus a slightly bigger amp rated at **80 W per channel (8 ohms, 20 Hz–20 kHz, 0.08% THD, two channels driven)**.

Everything else that matters is here: **seven channels** for 5.1.2 Atmos, **two independent subwoofer outputs**, HDMI inputs that pass **8K/60 and 4K/120**, eARC, HEOS, AirPlay 2 and a second zone. It's the receiver we'd point most people toward if their budget sits near the top of the affordable range.

The trade-off: like the S770H, it's a **7.2 processor**, so it can never run 5.1.4 even with an external amp. If you have any ambition beyond 5.1.2, the jump to the [Denon AVR-X3800H](/gear/denon-avr-x3800h/) in our [main receiver guide](/best-home-theater-receiver/) is the better long-term buy.

Compared with the [Onkyo TX-NR6100](/gear/onkyo-tx-nr6100/), the X1800H is easier to set up and has more polished streaming; the Onkyo has more power and Dirac. Both are strong picks for the best home theater receiver under $1,000 category.

The RX-V6A is Yamaha's 7.2-channel model and the pick for buyers who split time between movies and music. Yamaha rates it at **100 W per channel (8 ohms, 20 Hz–20 kHz, 0.06% THD, two channels driven)**, and it has **seven HDMI inputs** with HDMI 2.1 features including 4K/120 support (check which inputs carry it before plugging in a console).

**MusicCast** is the standout. It turns the receiver into part of a whole-home system with other Yamaha speakers and soundbars, with AirPlay 2, Spotify Connect and Bluetooth on top. **YPAO** calibration is straightforward and dependable, and Yamaha's on-screen setup is the friendliest of any budget receiver.

The trade-off: YPAO offers less control than Audyssey MultEQ XT or Dirac, and the RX-V6A is a 2020 design. Some early units of Yamaha's 2020 HDMI 2.1 receivers had a 4K/120 issue with the Xbox Series X that Yamaha addressed, so buy current stock and update firmware.

Against the [Denon AVR-X1800H](/gear/denon-avr-x1800h/), the Yamaha has more rated power (about 1 dB) and better multiroom music; the Denon has better calibration. Read our [Yamaha home theater review](/yamaha-home-theater-review/) for how it fits the wider lineup.

sections.heading: What a Budget Receiver Should Still Have
sections.body:
A cheap receiver is a good receiver if it keeps the four features that age worst when they're missing:

- **HDMI 2.1 with eARC.** eARC lets your TV send lossless Atmos from built-in apps to the receiver. HDMI 2.1 inputs let a PS5 or Xbox Series X run 4K/120 through it. See [HDMI 2.1](/glossary/hdmi-2-1/) and [eARC](/glossary/earc/).
- **Automatic room calibration.** Audyssey, YPAO, AccuEQ or Dirac. Even basic [room correction](/glossary/room-correction/) fixes speaker levels, distances and the worst bass peaks.
- **Two subwoofer outputs.** Even if you start with one sub, two outputs let you add a second later, the most effective bass upgrade there is.
- **Seven channels if you want Atmos.** Five channels can't drive height speakers. Seven gets you 5.1.2 [Dolby Atmos](/glossary/dolby-atmos/).

What you can safely give up on a budget: 11-channel processing, pre-outs for every channel, phono inputs, premium DACs and second-zone video. Those matter in a dedicated theater, not a first system.

sections.heading: Budget Power Ratings: Spotting the Inflated Number
sections.body:
Budget receivers are where power ratings get creative. Compare two ways of rating the same amp:

| Rating style | Load | Bandwidth | Distortion | Channels driven |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Full-bandwidth (FTC) | 8 ohms | 20 Hz–20 kHz | 0.05–0.1% | 2 |
| Headline / "max" | 6 ohms | 1 kHz | Up to 10% | 1 |

The [Onkyo TX-NR6100](/gear/onkyo-tx-nr6100/) is rated at 100 W the first way and 210 W the second. Neither number is a lie, but only the first is comparable across brands.

**Does a cheap receiver have enough power?** Usually, yes. A speaker with 87 dB [sensitivity](/glossary/speaker-sensitivity/) at a 3-meter seat gives about 77.5 dB from 1 W. At 75 W (the [Denon AVR-S770H](/gear/denon-avr-s770h/)), add 18.8 dB for roughly **96 dB per speaker**. Five speakers plus a subwoofer at that level is louder than most people ever listen. The gap from 75 W to 100 W is only 1.25 dB.

Where budget receivers struggle is with **4-ohm or very low-sensitivity speakers** in big rooms. Check your speakers' [impedance](/glossary/impedance/) before you buy.

sections.heading: How We Picked the Best Budget Home Theater Receiver
sections.body:
These rankings come from spec-sheet research, room maths and owner-reported reliability, not lab measurements. For budget models we weighted the criteria differently from our [main receiver guide](/best-home-theater-receiver/), because the question is what you lose by spending less:

1. **Must-have coverage.** Does it have HDMI 2.1, eARC, room calibration and streaming? The [Denon AVR-S770H](/gear/denon-avr-s770h/) won because it's the cheapest with all four plus Atmos heights.
2. **Channel count for the money.** Seven channels at a small premium over five ranks higher than five channels with extras you won't use.
3. **Room correction tier.** Dirac Live and MultEQ XT beat YPAO and basic MultEQ, which beat simpler auto-setup systems.
4. **Honest power.** Only full-bandwidth, two-channel ratings were compared.
5. **Support and reliability.** Firmware history, HDMI handshake complaints and how long the model has been supported.

A receiver that lacks Atmos and Wi-Fi (the [Sony STR-DH590](/gear/sony-str-dh590/)) can still earn a place if it's significantly cheaper and does the basics well.

sections.heading: What Each Price Tier Gets You
sections.body:
Street prices move constantly, so think in tiers rather than exact numbers:

**The cheapest tier (well under $500).** Expect 5.1 or 5.2, 4K/60 passthrough, Bluetooth and basic auto-setup. The [Sony STR-DH590](/gear/sony-str-dh590/) lives here. Fine for a TV and a speaker package; no Atmos heights.

**Around the $500 line.** This is where HDMI 2.1 and Wi-Fi appear. The [Yamaha RX-V4A](/gear/yamaha-rx-v4a/) (5.2) and, on sale, the [Denon AVR-S770H](/gear/denon-avr-s770h/) (7.2) are the models to watch. If you see one discounted, it's usually the best budget buy that week.

**Up to $1,000.** You get better room correction (MultEQ XT, Dirac Live), more power and more inputs. The [Denon AVR-X1800H](/gear/denon-avr-x1800h/), [Onkyo TX-NR6100](/gear/onkyo-tx-nr6100/) and [Yamaha RX-V6A](/gear/yamaha-rx-v6a/) are the best home theater receivers under $1,000.

**Up to $1,500–$2,000.** Nine amp channels and 11-channel processing arrive, which is where our [main guide's](/best-home-theater-receiver/) top pick, the [Denon AVR-X3800H](/gear/denon-avr-x3800h/), sits. It's only worth stretching if you plan on 5.1.4.

**Under $200–$300.** New receivers at this level usually lack HDMI entirely or are old stock. A discounted current model or a manufacturer-refurbished unit is a better bet than an unknown brand.

sections.heading: Five Channels or Seven on a Budget?
sections.body:
The practical question is whether height speakers will happen in your room.

**Choose a 5.2 receiver if:** your seating is against the back wall, your ceiling is vaulted or very low, or you're spending most of the budget on [speakers](/best-budget-home-theater-speakers/) and a [subwoofer](/best-budget-subwoofer-for-home-theater/). A good 5.1 system beats a mediocre 5.1.2 system every time.

**Choose a 7.2 receiver if:** you want Atmos now or later, or you have a deep room where rear surrounds make sense. The price gap between the RX-V4A and the S770H is small next to the cost of the speakers, and two up-firing modules on your front speakers are the cheapest way to add height effects.

One more option: if you're buying a TV at the same time, a 7.2 receiver running 5.1.2 typically outperforms a soundbar at the same total budget once you include a proper sub. Our [budget home theater system guide](/best-budget-home-theater-system/) covers full packages.

sections.heading: Setting Up a Cheap Receiver to Sound Expensive
sections.body:
Most of the difference between a cheap and an expensive system comes from setup, not hardware. Five steps that cost nothing:

1. **Set speakers to "Small" and the [crossover](/glossary/crossover/) to 80 Hz.** Let the subwoofer handle deep bass. It's the THX default and suits almost every bookshelf and many tower speakers.
2. **Calibrate properly.** Mic on a tripod at ear height, every position within the seating area, room quiet, sub gain at roughly the midpoint.
3. **Place the sub with the "crawl."** Put the sub at your seat, play bass-heavy content and crawl around the room; the spot with the smoothest bass is where the sub goes.
4. **Connect the TV via the eARC port** and turn on HDMI-CEC so one remote controls volume.
5. **Update firmware** before calibrating; HDMI and streaming fixes arrive this way.

Our [home theater setup guide](/home-theater-setup-guide/) walks through speaker placement for 5.1 and 5.1.2 in detail.

sections.heading: Who Should Buy a Budget Receiver, and Who Should Spend More
sections.body:
**A budget receiver is right if:** you're building your first surround system, your room is small to medium, your speakers are 6–8 ohms with average or better sensitivity, and 5.1 or 5.1.2 is your ceiling.

**Spend more if:** you have a dedicated room, want 5.1.4 or 7.1.4, plan to run two or more subwoofers with serious EQ, or have power-hungry 4-ohm speakers. The [Denon AVR-X3800H](/gear/denon-avr-x3800h/) or adding a [power amplifier](/best-home-theater-amplifier/) is the better route.

**Skip receivers altogether if** you can't run speaker wire to the back of the room. A [soundbar](/best-soundbar-for-home-theater/) with wireless surrounds is the simpler alternative.

mistakes.title: Buying an old 4K/60 receiver for a new console
mistakes.body: A very cheap older receiver will block 4K/120 and VRR if the console runs through it. Either buy HDMI 2.1 or plan to connect the console to the TV and use eARC.

mistakes.title: Choosing five channels when you want Atmos
mistakes.body: A 5.2 receiver decodes Atmos but has no outputs for height speakers. If overhead sound is the goal, seven channels is the minimum.

mistakes.title: Trusting the biggest number on the box
mistakes.body: Budget receivers often headline 1 kHz, 6-ohm, one-channel figures. Compare only the full-bandwidth, two-channel, 8-ohm rating.

mistakes.title: Pairing a budget receiver with 4-ohm speakers
mistakes.body: Many cheap AVRs are rated for 6–8 ohm loads. Hard-to-drive 4-ohm towers can make them run hot or shut down at high volume.

mistakes.title: Spending the subwoofer budget on the receiver
mistakes.body: In a budget system, a better sub makes a bigger audible difference than a better receiver. Keep money back for bass.

faqs.q: What is the best budget home theater receiver?
faqs.a: The Denon AVR-S770H is the best budget home theater receiver for most people because it combines 7.2 channels for 5.1.2 Atmos, HDMI 2.1 with 4K/120, eARC, Audyssey calibration and HEOS streaming. If you only need 5.1, the Yamaha RX-V4A is cheaper and also supports 4K/120.

faqs.q: Is a cheap AV receiver good enough?
faqs.a: Yes, for most living rooms. A current budget receiver with 75–100 W per channel (full-bandwidth, two channels driven), room calibration and HDMI 2.1 drives typical 6–8 ohm speakers to well over 90 dB at the seat. What you give up is expandability, advanced room correction and power for large rooms.

faqs.q: What is the best home theater receiver under $500?
faqs.a: Around the $500 mark, the Yamaha RX-V4A is the best 5.1 choice with 4K/120 HDMI and YPAO, and the Denon AVR-S770H is the one to watch for 5.1.2 Atmos when it's discounted. Below that, the Sony STR-DH590 covers basic 5.1 without Atmos or Wi-Fi.

faqs.q: What is the best home theater receiver under $1,000?
faqs.a: The Denon AVR-X1800H is the best home theater receiver under $1,000 for ease of use and Audyssey MultEQ XT, the Onkyo TX-NR6100 for Dirac Live and THX certification, and the Yamaha RX-V6A for multiroom music. All three are 7.2 receivers that run 5.1.2 Dolby Atmos.

faqs.q: How many watts do I need for a home theater receiver?
faqs.a: Most living rooms need 50–100 W per channel measured full-bandwidth into 8 ohms with two channels driven. With 87 dB speakers at a 3 m seat, 75 W gives about 96 dB per speaker, which is loud. Big rooms, 4-ohm or low-sensitivity speakers call for more power or an external amp.

faqs.q: Is Denon or Yamaha better for a budget receiver?
faqs.a: Denon is better if you want Atmos heights at the lowest price, since the AVR-S770H is a 7.2 receiver, and its Audyssey calibration has more tiers to upgrade into. Yamaha is better for a 5.1 system and for music, thanks to the RX-V4A's 4K/120 HDMI, simple YPAO setup and MusicCast multiroom.

faqs.q: Should I buy a refurbished receiver?
faqs.a: A manufacturer-refurbished receiver from Denon, Marantz, Yamaha or Onkyo is a good way to get a step-up model on a budget, usually with a warranty. Avoid unknown sellers, check the HDMI version, and update the firmware immediately. Amplifier sections are durable; HDMI boards are the usual weak point.

bottomLine: The **Denon AVR-S770H** is the best budget home theater receiver because it's the cheapest way to get 5.1.2 Atmos, HDMI 2.1, room calibration and streaming in one box. The **Yamaha RX-V4A** is the smarter buy for a 5.1 system with a console, and the **Sony STR-DH590** is the cheapest worthwhile receiver if you can live without Atmos and Wi-Fi. Spend a little more for the **Onkyo TX-NR6100** (Dirac Live), the **Denon AVR-X1800H** (Audyssey MultEQ XT) or the **Yamaha RX-V6A** (music and multiroom).

updates.note: Reorganized the page so the comparison table and how we chose come before the picks. Added a "skip it if" line on each pick, a sources section, notable mentions and a ranked table of every model we track in the category.

mentions.body: The Onkyo TX-NR5100 is an alternative to the [Denon AVR-S770H](/gear/denon-avr-s770h/) if you stream with Chromecast. It adds **Chromecast built-in** alongside AirPlay 2, and its 80 W/ch rating is only 0.28 dB above the Denon's 75 W, so choose on features, not watts. Its AccuEQ room correction offers less bass control than the Denon's Audyssey, so the S770H remains the better pick for most rooms.

The Sony STR-AN1000 is an alternative to the [Denon AVR-X1800H](/gear/denon-avr-x1800h/) for Sony TV owners. It adds **360 Spatial Sound Mapping** to widen a 5.1.2 layout, plus Chromecast built-in and Spotify Connect, but it sits in a slightly higher price band. Its 165 W headline is rated at 1 kHz, 10% THD with one channel driven, so it can't be compared with the Denon's figure, and Audyssey MultEQ XT keeps the Denon the better all-rounder.
